entry.title: COP31 climate talks expose deep divides over fossil fuels and finance
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / COP31 climate talks expose deep divides over fossil fuels and financeCOP31 climate talks expose deep divides over fossil fuels and finance

COP31's failure to reach a political agreement exposes deep divisions over fossil fuels and climate finance, putting global climate goals further at risk

premium

A COP31 sign is displayed at the venue of the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey. (Photo: Reuters)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 23 2026 | 10:01 PM ISTNo one was surprised when the 31st Conference of Parties (COP31) summit in Antalya, Turkey, ended without a central political agreement — the Antalya Pacts — despite running into two days of overtime. If anything, the longest-running climate talks in United Nations history highlighted the festering divisions between the developed and developing worlds over fossil fuels and climate finance. The result is that it is now clear that global temperatures are set to overshoot the Paris-Agreement target of holding temperatures below 1.5 degrees centigrade above pre-industrial levels — at a time when global temperatures broke new heat records this year. The draft pact sought to call on countries to keep the overshoot as low and for as short-lived a period as possible, a considerable dilution from the original Paris-Agreement pledges, and suggested carbon-capture storage as a substitute for cutting emission. The latter in itself is controversial; it works for some industries but is limited as an economically scalable solution.  But it was fossil fuels that proved a key deal breaker — although the pledge to transition away from fossil fuels was taken at COP28 in Dubai three years ago. The draft pact excluded all references to coal, oil and natural gas or transitioning away from fossil fuels, replacing it with anodyne phrasing on the “irreversible global transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development”. Refuting this framing was the European Union, the United Kingdom, Norway, small island-states and vulnerable states. This grouping was up against major oil- and gas-producing countries — most of them, not coincidentally, Turkish allies — as well as India, China, and Like Minded Developing Countries (LMDC). The other consequential point of disagreement was climate finance. A commitment to treble the figure by 2035 from $40 billion was articulated just last year. But the deepening North-South divide in climate talks means that the rich nations — the major historical contributors to global warming — were unwilling to commit to fixed contributions. At the same time, Russia accused developed nations of extending climate finance as loans rather than grants.  The 13 days of talks did record some gains, though the value of some of them is contestable. The proposed plan to raise electricity’s share in global consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 (the “35-by-35” deal) — which has morphed from a rigid mandate to a call for global cooperation — is one such. In countries such as China and India, for instance, the bulk of the electricity is generated through fossil fuels. At the same time, business deals worth $26 billion in agreements for renewables and grid pointed to some degree of momentum towards lowering greenhouse-gas emission. India’s low-key presence in Antalya reflected the shifting dynamics of climate talks. It continued to anchor its position in climate justice, Common But Differentiation Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities, equitable burden sharing, predictable finance for developing nation and an active opposition to climate-related trade barriers (such as Europe’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism). But it is notable that earlier this year, India withdrew its offer to host COP33 in 2028. As a result of the Antalya deadlock, many of the big issues will be carried over to COP32 in Addis Ababa next year.  Given the polarisation on the Turkish Riviera, consensus in a city on the edge of the Great Rift Valley looks just as unlikely.     Topics : Climate Change COP31 Global Warming Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: FPI disclosure rules need a wider review, not a response to outflows
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / FPI disclosure rules need a wider review, not a response to outflowsFPI disclosure rules need a wider review, not a response to outflows

FPI selling not only affected the equity markets but also put considerable pressure on the currency

premium

Representative Image for foreign portfolio investors (Photo: AdobeStock)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 23 2026 | 9:48 PM ISTThe Indian stock markets have suffered considerably because of selling by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs). Although FPIs have made a strong comeback, buying stocks worth over $14 billion on a net basis so far in November, they remain net sellers to the tune of over $17 billion since the beginning of the year. FPIs had also taken out about $18.9 billion in 2025 from the Indian stock markets. FPI selling not only affected the equity markets but also put considerable pressure on the currency. There are various explanations for FPI selling and their recent return. Aside from global factors such as the war in West Asia pushing up energy prices considerably, and money flowing from across the world to companies in the artificial-intelligence (AI) business and related areas, it is also argued that taxes and regulatory requirements are affecting flows into Indian markets.  In this context, the securities market regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi),  issued a consultation paper last week proposing the removal of the additional disclosure framework (ADF), which was introduced in 2023 for granular disclosures related to ultimate beneficial owners. The paper argues that many FPIs looking to invest in India see these disclosures as an additional compliance burden. Thus, instead of subjecting themselves to additional compliance, many investors may avoid investing in India. In effect, such requirements have become an entry barrier for FPIs. Under the current rules, if FPIs meet certain criteria on concentration or size, they have to submit granular details of all entities holding any ownership, economic interest, or exercising control in the FPIs up to the level of all natural persons without any threshold. Most jurisdictions don’t have such requirements.  The paper also highlights the stringent requirements under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, compared to other countries, though it is not in the regulator’s jurisdiction.  It is correct that in a world where capital is extremely mobile, it not only chases returns but also prefers markets where entry and exit are relatively easy. It is also reasonable to argue that India, which needs a sustained flow of foreign capital to supplement its domestic savings to achieve consistently high economic growth, should not be an outlier in terms of rules and regulations. In this regard, for example, a case is being made that capital gains made by FPIs should not be taxed in India as is the case in most parts of the world. It remains to be seen how this issue is settled. In the case of disclosures for FPIs, there is a need for a comprehensive review. Feedback on a consultation paper will not be enough simply because most stakeholders would not have full information. For instance, why was the additional disclosure framework introduced, what level of information has the regulator been collecting, and what has it done with that information? Similarly, why were the relevant provisions of the law against money laundering made more stringent in India than in other countries?  Therefore, what Sebi needs is an expert committee comprising officials from the regulator, law-enforcement agencies, and independent market experts. Such a committee will be in a position to examine all possible issues related to FPIs and present clear choices for both the regulator and government. Its report will also help inform public debate. Changes in rules and regulations should not be driven by the state of capital flows or prices on the ticker. They should be based on well-established and accepted principles.  This will also help provide stability and minimise changes.     Topics : SEBI Foreign Portfolio Investors FPIs Securities and Exchange Board of India Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Global tech outages expose need for stronger digital risk safeguards
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Global tech outages expose need for stronger digital risk safeguardsGlobal tech outages expose need for stronger digital risk safeguards

Opinions on the proximate causes differ but not all of these episodes were due to malicious cyberattacks. Perhaps none were. Most breakdowns have been attributed to buggy system updates

premium

Representative Picture

Business Standard Editorial Comment4 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 9:55 PM ISTIt has been an unusual 10 days, during which a string of apparently unconnected outages affected large swathes of the global economy, and even disrupted the networks at the United States’ (US’) digital-intelligence agency. On November 12, Microsoft’s systems went down, knocking out Outlook, Microsoft Teams, Copilot, SharePoint, and OneDrive, affecting individuals, educational institutions, governments and Fortune 500 companies. It took three days to restore services and the impact on global enterprise would run into billions of dollars. The company claims this was not caused by a cyberattack but a software bug and other technical issues. The next day, the US civil-aviation network went offline. All flights were disrupted within the US, spurring cancellations and rescheduling. Again, the losses would amount to billions. The issues may have started with router malfunctions, which led to the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) network being overwhelmed. A blame game is underway with the Democrats blaming the Republican administration for sacking hundreds of technical employees in civil aviation. On November 16 — last Monday — the US banking system suffered major downtime. The trouble apparently started with a software bug at JPMorganChase, which rippled through the interconnected financial system. Although this was apparently not due to an attack, cybercriminals took advantage of the confusion to carry out a heist, attacking cryptocurrency systems.  The day after this, Apple suffered an outage due to a buggy (a computer programme with bugs) software update. While that had a significant impact on enterprise, the news was subsumed by a crash in the internal network of the US National Security Agency due to “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance”. The underlying reasons for that “degradation” are likely to remain classified — some reckon it may also have been triggered by a buggy update.   Opinions on the proximate causes differ but not all of these episodes were due to malicious cyberattacks. Perhaps none were. Most breakdowns have been attributed to buggy system updates. It may be coincidental that all these occurred back-to-back. However, the disruption does highlight the fragility of the digital infrastructure underpinning the way the world functions. With artificial intelligence (AI) becoming more powerful and pervasive, the probability of such disruption is increasing. Naturally, many conspiracy theories are rife. However, even if malice is ruled out, it is obvious that there has been an explosion in critical vulnerabilities across global digital systems. AI algorithms and tools like the new Artex have also exposed a huge number of such vulnerabilities, and made it much easier to exploit them. Words like “vulnageddon” and “patchapocalypse” have been coined in this context to describe a nightmare scenario in which global systems go down in concatenated waves. These threats have forced organisations to roll out patches and updates to plug those gaps. And, doing this in haste may have led to a string of buggy updates, which are likely to lead to more such disruption.    The last few days may be considered a “live stress test” of the complex digital systems we daily use. While it led to losses, the toll could have been much worse. As we digitise and use AI, our vulnerabilities will increase with the dependencies. There is a need to review the extant and future vulnerabilities, including those holding up India’s digital public infrastructure. More robust disaster-recovery mechanisms have to be designed and rolled out, along with investment in redundant capacity across all domains. Given the legacy nature of most digital infrastructure, this period of technological instability implies massive investment and deep strategising to try and game out the potential weaknesses and ring-fence them.    Topics : Business Standard Editorial Comment BS Opinion Technology IT Industry

entry.title: PM Modi's criticism of industry calls for a two-way reform dialogue
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / PM Modi's criticism of industry calls for a two-way reform dialoguePM Modi's criticism of industry calls for a two-way reform dialogue

To take a systemwide view on the state of play between private capital and a government keen to stay out of doing business while fostering ideal conditions for more business

premium

Prime Minister Narendra Modi addresses the inaugural session of FICCI’s Annual General Meeting and Annual Convention. | Image credit: FICCI (X)

Business Standard Editorial Comment4 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 9:51 PM ISTThe next leap for India must begin with honest self-reflection, Prime Minister (PM) Narendra Modi last Thursday underlined in his address at the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (Ficci). Stressing that industry must reflect on its performance, the PM sent a strong message to captains of India Inc, rebuking them for having failed to do enough on job creation, wage increases, investment, and building capabilities to ramp up competitiveness and lowering import dependence. Mr Modi took on India Inc’s preoccupation with short-term growth riding on a captive domestic market, and what he termed an insatiable “appetite” of companies for the government doing the heavy lifting for them, be it in the form of cuts in corporation tax and tariff protections, or demand creation through reduction in personal income tax and goods and services tax, and new trade deals. For good measure, the PM reminded the members of Ficci, which is entering its 100th year, that Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi had delivered them a similar message in 1930, and rhetorically asked if his need to reiterate the need for self-reliance reflected industry’s success or failure.  There is much merit in the PM’s tough talk, and officials and ministers have been flagging some of these concerns for some time. The Economic Survey of 2024-25 had flagged that growth in wages and jobs has lagged growth in corporate profits, which hit a 15-year high in 2023-24. The Union finance minister, who had been urging private players to ramp up capex plans since the sharp cuts in corporation tax in late 2019, recently emphasised that the next phase of consumption growth hinged on companies paying employees more. While private capex has been slow to rev up, public capex has been propping up the investment cycle in recent years but there’s a limit to that stimulus. India Inc needs to step up its act if unemployment and stressed household budgets are a problem, especially if it prefers to continue to thrive on local demand. But the government needs to assess what makes employers reluctant to scale up, and why recent private capex has tended to be driven by a few large players in some capital-intensive sectors, and has not spread to employment-intensive smaller and medium enterprises. While the Centre has done its bit on easing and decriminalising provisions, expanding access to global markets, and simplifying taxation, disruption such as the pandemic, demonetisation or multiple wars has also affected investor visibility. As some industrialists noted, in a recently concluded series in this newspaper on 35 years of liberalisation, the regression towards higher import tariffs and non-tariff barriers like quality control orders has hurt prospects of global supply-chain integration for Indian firms. Production-linked incentives have worked patchily in most sectors, even as some sectors see fewer players dominate.    The PM is right — what has got India here won’t take it where it needs to be in 2047. It is in industry’s enlightened self-interest to plant and nurture the seeds of growth rather than bask in the safe pickings in walled gardens they have carved out through concessions and tariff protections. At the same time, the government must strive to hear and, more importantly, listen to what is holding investors back, not just at annual pre-Budget consultations with the finance ministry or other stakeholder talks held by line ministries on new policy ideas. To take a systemwide view on the state of play between private capital and a government keen to stay out of doing business while fostering ideal conditions for more business, it is perhaps time to revive a formal forum chaired by the PM himself, such as the erstwhile PM Council on Trade and Industry. Both stakeholders can then engage in some direct plainspeak every few months on expectations and reform wish lists, and, hopefully, chart a more frictionless path to prosperity.    Topics : Narendra Modi Business Standard Editorial Comment BS Opinion FICCI

entry.title: India must curb misleading health claims in booming nutraceuticals market
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / India must curb misleading health claims in booming nutraceuticals marketIndia must curb misleading health claims in booming nutraceuticals market

Misleading health claims in the growing nutraceutical market demand stricter regulation and stronger consumer protection

premium

The ASCI’s investigation found weight management to be the most prominent theme in advertisements, followed by skin care, anti-ageing, respiratory health and claims relating to specific diseases

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 19 2026 | 10:29 PM ISTThe Advertising Standards Council of India’s (ASCI’s) latest report, “A Pill for Thought”, highlights the risks of misleading health claims in India’s growing nutraceutical market. Of the 61 advertisements examined between July and September this year, all 60 completed cases violated the ASCI Code, while 31 advertisers failed to provide adequate evidence for their claims. The findings underline the need for stronger scrutiny of a market where false promises can have consequences for consumer health. The stakes are rising with the industry. According to one estimate, India’s nutraceutical market was valued at ₹3.67 trillion in 2025 and is projected to reach ₹8.05 trillion by 2033, growing at an annual rate of 10.3 per cent. Nutraceuticals, which include functional foods, fortified drinks, probiotics, vitamins and dietary supplements, occupy a space between food and pharmaceuticals. While these products can meet legitimate nutritional needs, their marketing must not exploit consumers’ health concerns.  The ASCI’s investigation found weight management to be the most prominent theme in advertisements, followed by skin care, anti-ageing, respiratory health and claims relating to specific diseases. Promises such as “Lose 6 kg in 60 days” and “Your thigh fat will be gone in 12 weeks” used before-and-after images to suggest predictable results. Some supplements and gummies positioned themselves as safer alternatives to prescription therapies. Such claims can create unrealistic expectations about the speed, extent and safety of the promised benefits. The problem extends beyond exaggerated weight-loss claims to claims reversing chronic diseases like asthma, obstructive pulmonary disease, blood pressure, cholesterol, and polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome.  The ASCI’s Annual Report for 2025-26 underlines the persistence of the problem. Nutraceuticals accounted for 52 per cent of food-and-beverage advertising cases, with 96 per cent requiring modification. The scale of violations suggests that existing mechanisms have not sufficiently deterred misleading claims. Although the ASCI’s self-regulatory framework can identify problematic advertisements and seek corrective action, its recommendations do not have the same force as statutory penalties. The rapid growth of digital advertising adds to the challenge. Influencers, sponsored content, and online marketplaces allow health claims to reach consumers quickly, often without the scrutiny applied to conventional advertisements.  India’s regulatory framework must, therefore, move beyond corrective action after an advertisement has appeared. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) and Central Consumer Protection Authority need to strengthen enforcement against unsupported health claims. The recent FSSAI advisory on mandatory labelling requirements and warnings for botanical ingredients underlines the need for greater scrutiny of product composition and safety information. Advertisers should be required to maintain credible, product-specific scientific evidence before making claims, rather than relying on studies of individual ingredients. Independent testing and transparent disclosure of the evidence supporting health benefits can help improve accountability. Penalties must be proportionate to the scale of the violation and the potential harm to consumers. Repeated violations should attract stronger consequences rather than a request to modify an advertisement. Stronger regulation and scientific scrutiny are essential to ensure that products sold in the name of wellness deliver what they promise.     Topics : ASCI health Editorial Comment Business Standard Editorial Comment

entry.title: India must turn China trade dependence into domestic value addition
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / India must turn China trade dependence into domestic value additionIndia must turn China trade dependence into domestic value addition

India must balance dependence on Chinese imports with domestic manufacturing growth and better access to China's market

premium

The government has realised that India’s own industrial ambitions require a certain openness to specialised imports from China

Business Standard Editorial Comment4 min read Last Updated : Nov 19 2026 | 10:20 PM ISTIndia’s bilateral trade deficit with China continues to grow, in a manner that will concern New Delhi. According to the recent data, in the first seven months of 2026-27, it reached a record $83 billion, 30 per cent higher than in the same period the previous financial year. There is real concern that, over the entire year, it could reach $150 billion. In 2025-26, it had touched $112 billion. It is worth noting, however, that the time of knee-jerk protectionism against Chinese imports is, in general, past. The government has realised that India’s own industrial ambitions require a certain openness to specialised imports from China. India’s electronics production and exports, particularly of mobile phones, have grown considerably in the past year. Much of that growth is dependent upon being part of supply chains that require inputs made in China. It should be noted, therefore, that a growing trade deficit with one country, particularly when it dominates the manufacturing space the way China does, is not necessarily deleterious if it supports India’s own attempts to build a space for itself in manufacturing and other value chains.  The question the government should, thus, ask itself is whether domestic value addition is dependent on other countries and whether supplier ecosystems are emerging within the country at sufficient scale. If that is indeed happening, then at least some of the trade deficit is amply justified. The other question that needs asking is a more difficult one. As the Union finance minister said in Bangkok during the annual meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund, the fundamental cause of the trade imbalance is that the Chinese market remains difficult to penetrate for Indian goods. She mentioned pharmaceuticals, among others, as a sector that was underperforming in terms of Indian exports to China.  This is not a problem that India alone faces. This is a global imbalance, caused by the fact that China’s state-led economy continues to artificially prioritise investment and production — and thus exports — over consumption. This is why its surplus in merchandise trade reached over $1 trillion in just the first 10 months of 2026, driven in part by growing exports of hi-tech goods that are needed to power the technological and artificial-intelligence transformation. If Chinese firms overinvest and create excess capacity, which then translates into low-cost exports, it is because the structure of their economy incentivises them to do so — through state support, directed credit, local-content preferences, and a slew of hidden and not-so-hidden subsidies. The weak purchasing power of Chinese households — caused by financial repression, quasi-administered wages, and an overdependence on the faltering real estate market as a store of wealth — doesn’t help.  This is not a problem, therefore, that New Delhi can easily solve on its own. It must continue to lobby for easier access to the Chinese market, but the bigger prize is to somehow speed up the internal transformation of the Chinese economy. This might require, in the end, multilateral efforts. It is unfortunate, however, that no attempt is being made at multilateral levels to directly address this. Leadership is required, and the natural candidate for it — the United States — is missing in action. President Donald Trump, who is now in China, is greatly concerned about trade imbalances but does not share this vision of how to address them. He would prefer to cut specific, sector-by-sector deals — but has so far largely failed to find any that stick. India must watch to see if any opening can be created for genuine multilateral action on this front — all while ensuring that its own unavoidable economic integration with China strengthens, and does not weaken, its position in global supply chains.     Topics : India china trade trade deficit China Indian exports Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: India can attract global capital if it removes barriers to investment
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India can attract global capital if it removes barriers to investmentIndia can attract global capital if it removes barriers to investment

Emerging-market investment is grounded in this promise. Indian asset prices have an imperfect correlation with the global portfolio and hence offer gains from diversification

premium

Illustration: Ajaya Mohanty

Ajay Shah6 min read Last Updated : Nov 22 2026 | 9:36 PM ISTEvery finance expert knows the power of diversification. We diversify across firms in an industry. We diversify across industries in a country. We diversify across countries. At each stage, we get a risk reduction. Harry Markowitz famously observed that diversification is the only free lunch observed in all economics. When a portfolio holds assets with uncorrelated returns, risk is quenched, and human welfare is enhanced.  This foundational logic provides the original basis for internationalised asset management. Cross-border capital flows create conditions in which all participants become better off through diversification and risk sharing. The desired state is where an Indian family owns a flat in Tokyo and rents it out to a resident while a Japanese family owns a flat in Bombay and rents it out to a resident. Each owner insulates the balance sheet from the home country risk. If India fares badly, the Tokyo asset continues to work well for the Indian owner, and vice versa. Each owner is well protected as compared to owning a flat in her or his own city. The pursuit of this protection, of this reduction of financial portfolio risk, drives capital across borders.  Emerging-market investment is grounded in this promise. Indian asset prices have an imperfect correlation with the global portfolio and hence offer gains from diversification. But their prices have to be driven down by market forces to compensate for the high risk of investing in India. Indian capital controls, taxation, policy risk, and the threat of expropriation by the state: All these drive up the required rate of return for a global investor to buy Indian assets (ie they drive down Indian asset prices). These policy choices act as a tax on capital, raising its cost. The central benefit for foreigners investing in India is the structural gain from diversification. The macroeconomic and political shocks in India are different from the shocks seen elsewhere, so investing in India is attractive.  Some unusual things happened in the past decade, and those complicated this pretty picture. There was a sustained big divergence, where the United States (US) economy did well and the Indian economy didn’t. The relevant metric for a global allocator is the dollar return, where depreciation in the exchange rate acts as a haircut on local equity gains. If we superpose the S&P 500 against the Indian Nifty 50, expressed in dollars, over the last nine years, we see that the Nifty grew from 100 to about 170. But the S&P 500 grew from 100 to 275. This is a large gap in performance: 6.44 per cent vs 11.48 per cent in dollars, on average. In these nine years, the gains from diversification into India went with a significant drag in average returns.  Nothing has changed in the finance theory! Diversification remains a free lunch. Financial markets process information efficiently. All information is contained in the price, so past performance is not relevant for future performance. The 95 per cent confidence interval for the annual S&P 500 return, based on this data, runs from —1.09 per cent to 25.65 per cent and for the Nifty it is — 5.42 per cent to 19.78 per cent: Hardly a strong foundation to make claims about the future. But such a performance gap over a nine-year period weighs on many practical people. The curious combination of superior US stock-market performance with sluggish Indian stock-market performance, over a nine-year period, has had a force of its own.  While financial markets are quite efficient, decision making in financial intermediation is often less than rational. Asset allocators operate in institutional settings defined by investment committees and career risk. The theoretical mandate to diversify, to not care about past performance, clashes with the institutional pressure to chase the assets that recently outperformed.  This unique backdrop has generated a drag against foreign investment into India. When the dominant global asset class delivers exceptional returns, the appetite to underwrite the institutional frictions of emerging markets diminishes. The bar for the entry of foreign capital rises, and the flow of global savings into Indian assets faces a structural headwind.  We should not overstate the macroeconomic problem caused by this dynamic. Sanjuktha Athreya demonstrated that it was a stall, not a reversal (https://bit.ly/IndiaStall). Capital did not flee, but it stopped arriving at the previous rate. The macroeconomic impact of this stall was muted by domestic conditions. There was poor corporate investment in India in this period. The macroeconomic identity links the current-account deficit to the gap between domestic investment and domestic savings. Because corporate capital expenditure was weak, the demand for capital was low, so the gap between investment and savings in India was weak. Consequently, there was no great need for inflows of foreign capital. The economy did not face a financing constraint that foreign savings had to resolve, so softness in capital inflows was not a problem.  If artificial intelligence and tech fever in US asset pricing cools, this could potentially induce global investors think about international portfolio formation in a more normal way. A moderation in US equity returns would assist allocators in returning to more orthodox, more theoretically sound strategies. It would restore the traditional focus on international diversification and the pursuit of uncorrelated returns across global markets. This would be good for India.  If foreign investors took more interest in India — and if the Indian authorities removed policy mistakes that impede inflows of foreign capital — then there would be a greater interest in Indian assets. This would exert a causal impact on Indian economic growth through the following path. First, Indian asset prices would go up. For example, when foreigners take an interest in India (and the Indian authorities do not come in the way), Indian corporate bond yields go down. Second, firms would find more investment projects attractive when asset prices are higher. A firm with a high price-earning ratio does more investment than a firm with a low one; a firm with a cheap cost of debt does more investment than a firm with high cost of debt. Such a surge of investment would help growth in gross domestic product. Equal treatment for foreigners by the Indian state remains a powerful lever to push Indian economic growth, and it’s not that hard to do.  
The writer is a researcher at XKDR Forum     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : BS Opinion Investment Emerging market countries

entry.title: India Inc must summon the courage to challenge government policy openly
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India Inc must summon the courage to challenge government policy openlyIndia Inc must summon the courage to challenge government policy openly

One big cause of Mr Modi's frustration is corporate India's unwillingness to pass on the benefits of tax cuts to employees through raises, hiring, or investment

Prime Minister Narendra Modi addresses the inaugural session of FICCI’s Annual General Meeting and Annual Convention. | Image credit: FICCI (X)

Shekhar Gupta7 min read Last Updated : Nov 21 2026 | 10:12 AM ISTThe most apt description for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s mass admonition of corporate India at the Ficci annual general meeting is that it was a cri de coeur. I use this even as I’m reminded of the late and venerable D N Singh, my first news editor at The Indian Express in 1977. He had banned “foreign” words in our writing. English is foreign enough for all of us, he’d say. In this case, however, a cry from the heart doesn’t fully capture where the Prime Minister was coming from. The dictionary tells us that a cri de coeur is more profound. It’s a “passionate, heartfelt appeal, protest, even an outcry”. The Prime Minister spoke in anger, frustration, helplessness even. What more can I do to get you guys moving? It was way more fraught than a mere cry from the heart.  It’s a bit like a general failing to implore his troops to assault a hill despite a thousand war cries, words of inspiration, even a dash of “spirit”. Since we started with a bit of French, that “spirit” reference is from the Duke of Wellington at the Battle of Waterloo. While his original line, as recorded in history, was less dramatic, Christopher Plummer, playing Wellington in the 1970 film Waterloo, tells the Duchess of Richmond, who wants to know where his troops get their inspiration to fight: “Gin is the spirit of their patriotism.” I’m avoiding the full quote because the Prime Minister certainly didn’t want to call corporate India ‘scum, beggars and scoundrels,’ as Wellington called his troops. It’s just that his frustration is as profound.

Also Read

Doing our bit: India Inc responds to PM's wake-up call on jobs and pay

PM 'rattled', realised he will be 'outgoing PM' soon, says Congress

Nepal PM's 2-day India visit: Rail link, trading post on the cards

Technology created vistas for cultural connectivity, says PM Modi

Wife brand vs Mistress Brand: Can public status outweigh private utility?premium

 What’s the spirit that a government can offer entrepreneurship? It can be many things: Deregulation, minimum government, fair market supervision, fiscal discipline, freedom from licensing and investment restrictions. And certainly, the gin equivalent of this “spiritual” package would be tax cuts. One big cause of Mr Modi’s frustration is corporate India’s unwillingness to pass this benefit on to employees through raises, hiring or investment. This hasn’t happened even as corporate profits have risen. These troops are unwilling, either too scared to assault that hill or simply too comfortable in safety, pocketing the tax breaks. Let’s read some of Mr Modi’s words to Ficci. “In 2014, the basic corporate tax rate was 30 per cent. We reduced it to 22 per cent. Today, there’s no income tax on earnings up to ~12 lakh in India.” And then he turns the knife. “I know you won’t clap, because however much one gives, your appetite never seems to be satisfied. (aap ka pet nahin bharta). Did you increase the salaries of your employees? Did you increase the number of employees? No. The attitude remains: ‘Modi ji, you do it, we will see’.” While India Inc was left licking its wounded pride, the Congress quickly latched on to the Prime Minister’s words. Isn’t this what we’ve been saying all along, it hit back. Jairam Ramesh was first out of the blocks. “For the first time in 12 years, a nervous and rattled PM has pulled up the captains of industry... (who) must have been taken aback and shocked.” In an elaborate post on X, he blamed not businesses but the government for this stall. He blamed it on crony capitalism, regulatory capture, “an atmosphere of fear and intimidation”, and the unleashing of “investigative agencies”. He concluded by suggesting the Prime Minister look inwards. Rahul Gandhi, on his speaking tour in the United States, also said: We told you so. It’s not my place here to hold forth on the state of the economy. But we know corporate India hasn’t been investing, expanding and hiring, at least nowhere near what 7 per cent-plus growth would indicate. Startups are rising, but largely there’s an entrepreneurship freeze. Much of the growth comes from government spending, especially in heavy infrastructure. If corporate India looks so risk-averse, this isn’t a sudden development. The mood has been festering for years. Some complain of a lack of demand, others say regulation is asphyxiating. Still too many forms need to be filled for too many small things, even something as virtuous as exports. Because, I suppose, the Reserve Bank of India wants to track every dollar that comes in. And, of course, everything in triplicate please. The government may have loosened policies here and there, but the bureaucratic grip is tighter than before. A quick quiz, and no Googling. Can you name the ministers of mines, pharmaceuticals and steel? I mention these three because the Prime Minister highlighted corporate India’s failures specifically in these areas. Why do we export raw materials like iron ore, have so much bauxite, yet import finished steel and specialised aluminium alloys? How come, despite robust pharma exports, we remain dependent on China for APIs, or active pharmaceutical ingredients? With key ministers too lightweight or distracted by party work, and power centralised in the PMO, which is obviously far too overburdened to attend to everything, discretion devolves to the bureaucracies. Corporate India is resigned to this. It’s buying peace in the manner it knows best: Distributing some of the spoils in a way that’s entirely legal and above board, but also revealing. Check out the number of retiring secretaries, especially in the finance ministry, finding sinecures on the boards of influential companies and as chairpersons of almost all significant private-sector banks, and the recently listed stock market titan, NSE (National Stock Exchange). The more the Modi government thinks it’s reforming — and reforming it is — the more it does so in a way that passes power into the hands of the bureaucracy. Corporate India buys peace with them in advance, merely by dropping hints. Here’s the paradox. This is a super-strong government with a very weak implementation spine. As a result, what’s decentralised at the top gathers in the middle. A strong government isn’t immune to policy confusion. On the contrary, it can be prone to flip-flop-flips given its overwhelming power. Long term capital gains (LTCG) tax is a big discussion point now. Count how many changes this government has brought in. The same goes for taxes on dividends. Since 1991, successive finance ministers have said that the essence of a reformed economy lies in moderate, predictable taxes. You most certainly cannot say the same about this government, which also taxes individuals at almost twice the rate of corporations. It’s also been breathtaking in its use of sovereign power. A striking example is the retrospective changes it made to sovereign gold bonds to suit itself and cover for those brilliant people who floated these without hedging for gold prices. The message is an old one. In India, the government, the almighty Sarkar-e-Hind, can never be wrong. Corporate India has a lot to answer for, but for some, the chappal is on the government’s foot. On copper and aluminium imports, two of the largest projects have been shut under activist pressure. If this government has failed to move on these, it cannot blame India Inc. Sadly, corporate India knows this, but nobody would dare speak up. They whisper dark things on the sidelines. But in front of an angry Prime Minister, or the finance minister who’s been delivering the same admonitions for two years, they sit silent and contrite, like schoolkids whose homework the dog ate. This isn’t just a Modi-era phenomenon. At the 2007 CII AGM, then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh had chided corporate leaders for paying themselves too much. The irony: The mood and message then were opposite to now. Sunil Mittal, then CII chief, responded by pledging ‘a significant part of his salary bonus’ to charity. I had then written, and repeated in a 2013 column, that corporate India has to grow the spine to tell the Prime Minister he didn’t fix their wages. He should leave them alone if they paid their taxes honestly. Of course, no such thing happened. Corporate India also swallowed that retrograde idea of near-mandatory corporate social responsibility. Even at Ficci, and in the corporate and financial universe, too many good people have too many important points to make. But nobody would dare. Corporate India is waiting for its next Rahul Bajaj. Or preferably a few of them.

entry.title: Wife brand vs Mistress Brand: Can public status outweigh private utility?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Wife brand vs Mistress Brand: Can public status outweigh private utility?Wife brand vs Mistress Brand: Can public status outweigh private utility?

Indians buy one brand to impress the world and another to live their lives. Most brands do not understand this

premium

Ask a man in Gurugram what watch he wears. He will say, “Rolex.” That’s his Wife Brand | Image Credit: Bloomberg

Sandeep Goyal5 min read Last Updated : Nov 20 2026 | 10:57 PM ISTThere are two kinds of brands in our lives. The Wife Brand and The Mistress Brand.  The Wife Brand is the one you marry. You show her off. You introduce her to your parents, to your boss, to society. She has pedigree. She is expensive. She looks good in photos. You bought her after a lot of research and after taking a loan.  The Mistress Brand is the one you actually love spending time with. She is comfortable. She is fun. She doesn’t judge you. She is there for you every day, at home, when no one is watching. You didn’t take out a loan for her. You just picked her up because she made you feel good.  One is for log kya kahenge (what will people say?). The other is for mujhe kya chahiye (what do I want?).  Ask a man in Gurugram what watch he wears. He will say, “Rolex.” That’s his Wife Brand. Now ask him what watch he wears when he goes for a morning walk. It is a G-Shock. Or an Apple Watch. That is his Mistress Brand.  The Wife Brand is for the boardroom. The Mistress Brand is for the bedroom.  Women do it too. Every woman has a Wife Brand handbag — Louis Vuitton, never out of its dust bag, used only for weddings and kitty outings. And a Mistress Brand handbag — Zara tote, or that big Fabindia jhola that goes everywhere. She loves the jhola. She respects the LV.  This is the most powerful, most unspoken truth of Indian consumer behaviour. And most brands never understand it. We are a country of two-brand lives.  We buy an Apple iPhone — that's the Wife. We flaunt it on Instagram. But our second phone, the one with two SIMs and a big battery for the driver and the house help to call, is a OnePlus or a Xiaomi. That’s the Mistress. Nearly 70 per cent of iPhone users in India also own an Android. Apple will never tell you this.  We buy Nike shoes — Wife Brand. ~12,000. For the gym photos. But for the daily 5 km walk in the park? Skechers. Or Bata. Comfortable, soft, no one will judge. Nike is for society. Skechers is for the soul. That’s why Skechers sells more pairs in India than Nike, even though Nike spends 10 times more on advertising.  We even eat this way.  Olive oil is the Wife Brand. We keep the bottle in front of the kitchen so guests can see. We use it when the nutritionist comes. But the daily tadka? Fortune refined oil. Or desi ghee. The Mistress Brand that actually makes the food taste good. Olive oil is respect. Ghee is love.  Why does the Wife exist then? Because India is still a status society. We don’t buy brands only for ourselves. We buy brands for our neighbours, our relatives, our office colleagues.  A Rolex doesn’t tell time better. It tells people your time has come. A Mercedes doesn’t drive better in Gurugram traffic. It tells people you have arrived, even if you haven't moved 100 meters in 30 minutes.  Wife Brands are signal brands. They signal success, taste, arrival. But Mistress Brands are utility brands. They work. They are loyal.  And here is the marketing secret no one tells you: Wife Brands make the noise. Mistress Brands make the money.  So what should a brand want to be? Being a Wife Brand is expensive. You have to spend all the time to stay beautiful. You have to do ads with Alia Bhatt. You have to be on the cover of Vogue.  Mistress Brands are resilient. No one cares if Skechers didn’t do an ad with Ranveer. No one trolls Bata.  The smartest brands in the last 10 years chose to be Mistresses, not Wives.  Look at Zudio. Zudio never said, “We are premium.” Zudio said, “We are your daily wear.” It is the ultimate Mistress Brand to Zara’s Wife Brand. Zara is where you go to impress. Zudio is where you go to live. Today Zudio sells more than Zara and H&M combined.  If you are a Wife Brand, accept it. Spend money. Stay beautiful. Be ready for judgement. And know that you will be loved in public, but maybe not used every day.  If you are a Mistress Brand, stop trying to become the Wife. Stop doing luxury ads. Stop hiring that expensive agency. Embrace your role. Be comfortable. Be available. Be affordable. Be there at 11 pm when they need you.  People stay for the Wife.  But they live for the Mistress.  
The writer is chairman, Rediffusion   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : BS Opinion Branding Brands

entry.title: PM Balendra Shah's brief Delhi visit unfolds amid Nepal's domestic strains
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / PM Balendra Shah's brief Delhi visit unfolds amid Nepal's domestic strainsPM Balendra Shah's brief Delhi visit unfolds amid Nepal's domestic strains

By temperament, Mr Shah is not a consensus man, nor is diplomacy his forte. This makes structural reform via legislation a bit harder

premium

Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri during a meeting with Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah, in Kathmandu.(Photo:PTI)

Aditi Phadnis5 min read Last Updated : Nov 20 2026 | 10:53 PM ISTWhen Nepal Prime Minister (PM) Balendra Shah (36) arrives in India on November 22 on his first state visit, it will be the briefest bilateral sojourn in New Delhi by any PM from that country: He leaves on November 23, without taking up the government’s offer of showing him around Bengaluru, Ahmedabad, Ayodhya, or Varanasi.  But for the 25 hours he is in New Delhi, Mr Shah will leave domestic worries behind. He took office eight months ago, on the back of the stupendous electoral victory of the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), popularised by its election symbol, the ghanti (bell). From 11 seats in the last general election, the RSP shot up to 182 in a 275-member house in the 2026 poll, just two short of a two-thirds majority. The irony is that even with this order of seats, the government is hobbled: Zero seats in the Upper House or in any of the provinces. The next set of elections to the Upper House is scheduled for 2028. So, till then, only those reforms on which there is a political consensus are likely to become law. By temperament, Mr Shah is not a consensus man, nor is diplomacy his forte. This makes structural reform via legislation a bit harder. To make up for this, the government has tended to resort to optics to showcase its work: The arrest of former Prime Minister K P Sharma Oli and former home minister Ramesh Lekhak, for instance, or the attempted arrest of Nepali Congress leader and former Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba on charges of money laundering, nixed because of legal infirmities.  This could be because Mr Shah’s Cabinet is the youngest in Nepal’s history and only two of its 17 members have ministerial experience. Expectations are high, but promises made during the campaign are nowhere near fulfilment. The most consequential among them is land reform, specifically land ownership certificates, called Lalpurja (because of the red paper on which they are printed). Like in India, not all tillers of land are certified owners. They may have owned the land for generations but without a valid, verified Lalpurja. There’s simply no legally recognised property ownership in Nepal. Banks won’t approve loans against unverified land. Government offices won’t process transfers. Courts won’t uphold ownership claims without it. This is one reason for the infancy of Nepal’s real-estate sector. But there is also politics. Lalpurja was a signal promise of the RSP during the elections. But given his background as mayor of Kathmandu and his ruthless action against squatters and encroachment, Mr Shah has indeed ordered clearing squatters but has paid scant attention to how these families should be re-housed. If this is ignored (many so-called squatter families are currently housed in camps) the mood could turn against the ghanti very quickly.  Corruption is another serious problem. Tiny Lame Ahal village, just outside Pokhara, one of Nepal’s biggest tourist destinations, used to be conservative and determinedly pro-Nepali Congress. At 50-something, Ganga Gurung is not a typical ghanti supporter. Ghanti supporters tend to be younger. But she says dramatically: “Even if you hold a pistol to my head, I will vote Ghanti. They opened our eyes.” Although party chief Rabi Lamichhane has cases of corruption against him (he was in prison when “liberated” by a mob that led to Mr Oli’s resignation), there is no movement on those files. Scandals involving “fixers” and the rigging of courts abound.  Existential problems continue. Lack of employment has been exacerbated by the return of migrant workers from West Asia. In March this year alone, of the three million who work in the region, around 6,000 Nepali workers had applied online to return home. The remittances these migrants sent back to Nepal represent more than a third of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP) and some of them could now need to find employment at home. Natural disasters have added another dimension to the management of emergencies in Nepal.  That foreign policy is not a priority for the Shah government is understandable though appearing to balance the interests of India and China in the region is crucial if Nepal wants to be left in peace. When he comes to India, the two sides are likely to unveil a 10-year vision document: A peek at this reveals nothing new. The two most contentious areas — India’s Agniveer scheme and the recruitment challenge it represents for Nepal; and differences on the delineation of the border — are unlikely to come any closer to resolution during this trip. Nepal’s attention is also divided: When the PM is in India, a large high-ranking parliamentary delegation will be in China at the invitation of the Chinese Communist Party at the same time. Although China has been courting Nepal with its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), financing for it is yet to come.  The unknown element is the role of the United States (US) in Nepal. In the past, US policy used to be influenced by India’s stance. This is gradually changing, though Kathmandu is wary of riling New Delhi on this score.  For Mr Shah, being different is crucial. The outcome to look out for is whether New Delhi acknowledges this.   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: India must rethink aviation strategy to make airlines commercially viable
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India must rethink aviation strategy to make airlines commercially viableIndia must rethink aviation strategy to make airlines commercially viable

Is there really a case for expanding Indian aviation when even a near-monopoly airline slips into losses at the slightest adverse turn in costs?

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

R Jagannathan6 min read Last Updated : Nov 20 2026 | 10:40 PM ISTSomeone once noted that India has low-fare airlines, not low-cost ones. This is because the cost structures unique to domestic airlines relate to inflexible ones like high fuel prices and taxes, aircraft leasing charges, and high landing and parking charges at major airports.  You can run a low-cost airline only if you have special cost advantages, which practically no domestic airline has. Indigo, at some point, seemed to have cracked the code for ensuring high efficiency on relatively low fares, but today — despite having two-thirds of the Indian aviation market and without any real airfare constraints — it is reporting losses.  While the quarterly losses are directly related to the two wars that have pushed up fuel costs for everyone, the point is this: If even a near-monopoly airline keeps making losses the minute some cost factor turns unfavourable, where is the case for expanding Indian aviation phenomenally? And Air India, nearly five years after privatisation, is nowhere near breaking even.  Consider a few facts. One, despite a massive surge in the creation of new airports, including under the UDAN scheme, some reports note that around 15 airports are either non-functional or unviable, given current traffic levels. With land pricey, and security costs only growing in a world full of challenges from non-state terrorist actors, overall airport costs are only going to rise.  This means airport costs for airlines will not come down anytime soon.  Two, low-cost airlines need low-cost infrastructure and much lower fuel prices, but that is not going to happen in India when both Centre and states rely heavily on revenues from fuel taxation to meet budgetary needs.  Three, the main factor supporting the growth of aviation is speed of travel between two cities. But most cities do not have the necessary connectivity from city to airports, making the actual cost and time taken to travel much greater than what the headline says. The waiting time for passengers at most airports is also very high, given delays and security needs.  Four, the rapid expansion of high-speed rail, possibly over the next 10 years, will make short-distance air travel a less enticing option. Railways Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw has gone on record to say that 99 per cent of short-distance travel will be done by rail, and airlines had better watch out.  Five, far-flung places like the Northeast will still require airline services, but these cannot happen without large and repeated state subsidies. Defence needs will also necessitate heavy subsidies for airports in these regions.  India needs to rethink its airline and airports strategy so that it starts making commercial and social sense. The question: Why do we keep investing so much in a sector that, with the smallest of disruptions, seems likely to go into losses and in need of government support? The International Air Transport Association sees the global airline industry’s net profit margin dropping by half to 2 per cent in 2026, thanks to the various disruptions. And even this gross margin figure hides the real state of the industry. Most airlines are probably under water.  This is not to suggest that India should not be investing in aviation, but it must rethink how it can do so smartly. When gestation periods are so high, why should we be investing in a sector with such low returns?  So what do we need to rethink?  First, we should not allow any new airport to come up without actually building the infrastructure and connectivity for it. This goes not only for small airports in the hinterland, but also for airports in high-density routes. Consider how long it takes to travel from Bengaluru’s software hub in Electronics City to the new airport. One has to add at least two hours each way for the journey to the airport, and a further hour at the landing end. This is more than the time spent in the air.  Consider also the extreme reluctance of airlines to shift from Terminal 1 in Mumbai (which is to be rebuilt) to Navi Mumbai. Poor connectivity is possibly the only reason despite the fact that the new airport offers better facilities than the old terminal in Santacruz/Vile Parle.  Two, there is a need to liberalise policy to allow domestic ones to fly more abroad, since there is little chance of fuel costs being cut for operations within India. The five-year domestic operation norm before getting permission to fly abroad has been abandoned, but airlines must operate at least 20 aircrafts on domestic routes to fly abroad. Why is this rider needed when most airlines believe that international routes offer them a better yield per passenger, given the opportunity to buy fuel at lower costs abroad?  Assuming our overall people and other non-fuel costs are lower than what is the norm globally, won’t Indian airlines benefit from flying more between third countries? This may mean negotiating seventh freedom rights (which allow airlines to operate between any two countries without having a home connection) for Indian airlines, which would also imply allowing airlines based abroad to operate between India and other destinations. What we could do is to allow this only if foreign airlines fly to underutilised large airports like Noida or Navi Mumbai and make them alternative hubs.  Three, we need stripped down airports with very low costs (just a runway, one coffee shop and security) in order to allow real low-cost airlines to emerge at some point. The existing rule, which does not allow a greenfield airport to be set up within a 150-km radius of an existing civilian airport, makes this unlikely, though exceptions have been made. The logical thing to do is to negotiate lower revenue shares from airport operators on high-density private airports like Delhi in order to get them to give greater concessions on their monopoly rights. Given the extraordinary amount of time needed to travel to the airport through congested roads, we need more airports closer to city centres. Bengaluru’s software hub would be better served with a basic airport near Hosur in Tamil Nadu than by building another one far away from the city in a completely different direction.  Net-net: Many operators entered the airline business looking at it as a trophy business (Vijay Mallya, for example), when in reality it is an albatross for those without deep pockets and patient capital. It is time to change the rules of the game and the policy framework underpinning it. The space must be opened up for competition, while, at the same time, safeguarding the interests of established domestic players.

entry.title: Time in a bottle: Voyager's Golden Records may outlive humanity itself
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Time in a bottle: Voyager's Golden Records may outlive humanity itselfTime in a bottle: Voyager's Golden Records may outlive humanity itself

the Voyagers will be dead, and the people who built them will be gone. The records, which need no electricity, may outlast us all

premium

Voyager 1, launched on September 5, 1977, has gone farther than anything humans have made | Photo: Nasa

Kumar Abishek5 min read Last Updated : Nov 20 2026 | 10:16 PM ISTLong before Chandrayaan and Mangalyaan, a fragment of India was already en route to leave the solar system. It was the voice of Kesarbai Kerkar, a great Hindustani singer. Recorded in then Bombay in April 1953, her three-and-a-half-minute Jaat Kahan Ho, in raga Bhairavi, was chosen for the Golden Record aboard the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s (Nasa’s) Voyager spacecraft. The title asks: “Where are you going?” — an apt question for a machine bound for eternity.  Kerkar died on September 16, 1977, 11 days after Voyager 1 left Earth. Her voice, though, kept going, carrying a morning raga into a darkness where there are no mornings.  On November 18, Voyager 1 was one light-day from Earth, about 25.9 billion kilometres. A radio signal, travelling at the speed of light, needs 24 hours to cross it. In other words, every conversation with our farthest emissary now has a two-day pause in the middle.  Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977, and has gone farther than anything humans have made. It passed Jupiter and Saturn, then slipped into interstellar space in 2012, moving at about 17 kilometres per second. Voyager 2, launched on August 20, 1977, gave humanity its only close-up views of Uranus and Neptune. It entered interstellar space in 2018. Its one-light-day milestone is expected in November 2035.  Both are beyond the heliosphere, the Sun’s vast magnetic bubble of charged particles.  Each carries the same Golden Record, a 12-inch gold-plated copper disc meant for whatever intelligence might one day find it. It is Earth in a time capsule: 115 images, greetings in 55 languages (several of them Indian), and some 90 minutes of music. There are birds calling, surf breaking, thunder, a heartbeat, a baby crying, a kiss, and even the recorded brain waves of Ann Druyan, who co-wrote the 1980 PBS documentary series Cosmos hosted by Carl Sagan, the legendary American astronomer who led the team that put the record together and whom she later married. Her brain waves were captured while she meditated on love and Earth. Alongside Bach, Beethoven and folk music from different parts of the world sits Kerkar’s voice from India.  Sagan’s team faced a harder problem than gathering sounds: How to teach a stranger who had never met human technology to play them. Their answer, etched into the aluminium cover, was an instruction manual written in physics. A diagram of the hydrogen atom’s spin-flip transition supplies a universal unit of time, so a clever finder can decode the playback speed: One rotation every 3.6 seconds. Other diagrams show how to rebuild the pictures, starting with a plain circle. A map places the Sun among 14 pulsars, a cosmic address that allows even for their slowing. A speck of uranium-238 serves as a clock; its half-life could reveal the record’s age.  It is an ingenious attempt to speak across language, culture and time. Would anyone understand? The finder might have no phonograph, or hear in ways we cannot imagine. The record is an invitation, not a message with a guaranteed reader.  The Voyagers are running out of time. Their plutonium-238 generators lose about four watts a year, and engineers have spent years switching off instruments and heaters to make what remains last. Voyager 1 still runs a magnetometer and a plasma-wave detector; Voyager 2 adds a cosmic-ray detector.  This year, engineers found another way to extend their lives. The “Big Bang” operation switched off three relatively power-hungry devices for lower-power alternatives, while keeping the craft warm. Completed on Voyager 2 in July and Voyager 1 in September, it extended the remaining instruments’ lives into the early 2030s.  Still, power will eventually drop too low, or something will fail first: A clogged thruster line, a memory glitch, an antenna slowly losing its aim at a Sun-sized dot. Yet, the spacecraft will keep moving, unpowered and unobserved.  In three centuries, Voyager 1 will reach the Oort Cloud’s inner edge, then take 30,000 years to cross its shell of icy objects. In around 40,000 years, it will pass within 1.6 light-years of Gliese 445, also catalogued as AC+79 3888, in Camelopardalis, a large constellation of the Northern Sky representing a giraffe. Voyager 2 will pass similarly close to Ross 248.  Pioneers 10 and 11 — the first two spacecraft to escape the solar system into interstellar space – are, meanwhile, silent. New Horizons, though, is alive and travelling through the Kuiper Belt.   Other journeys are imagined. Johns Hopkins’ Applied Physics Laboratory has designed an Interstellar Probe concept several times faster than Voyager. China has explored similar proposals. Breakthrough Starshot, founded by Yuri Milner, Stephen Hawking, and Mark Zuckerberg, dreams of laser-driven sails racing towards Alpha Centauri, the closest star system to our solar system.   For now, the Voyagers are humanity’s only active emissaries beyond the heliosphere.  One day, the Voyagers will be dead, and the people who built them will be gone. The records, which need no electricity, may outlast us all. Sagan called them bottles thrown into the cosmic ocean. The odds anyone will play one are tiny.  But if someone does, they will find a portrait of humankind, a snapshot of who we hoped to be in 1977: A species capable of making a mother’s lullaby, a Bach fugue, and a Bhairavi alap. Long after the signal fades, the music will carry on. Somewhere in that quiet, an old Hindi voice will ask: Where are you going? Will it find an answer?

entry.title: Time-limited, auctioned export quotas beat blanket trade restrictions
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Time-limited, auctioned export quotas beat blanket trade restrictionsTime-limited, auctioned export quotas beat blanket trade restrictions

The EU-China export deal to protect European carmakers is a compromise but preferable to a prohibitive tariff

Chinese electric and hybrid cars amid EU-China trade restrictions (Representative Image)(Image Credit: Bloomberg)

Shang-Jin Wei5 min read Last Updated : Nov 19 2026 | 11:33 PM ISTThe European Union and China have reportedly agreed to limit Chinese hybrid-car exports to Europe. According to Bloomberg, the deal would cap exports at about 350,000 vehicles a year, with the cap rising by 6 per cent annually. The restriction would take the form of a voluntary export restraint (VER) by China. Who wins and who loses from such an arrangement, and should VERs serve as a template for future agreements on how to manage trade conflicts? To answer this question, we have to go back to 1981. Under American pressure, Japan agreed to limit its car exports to the United States to 1.7 million a year. The cap was called “voluntary” so the US could maintain the façade of adherence to free trade. With exports capped, Japanese carmakers raised prices, moved upmarket, and invested the resulting profits. American consumers paid $1,500-$2,500 more per car, yet the restriction remained in place until 1994.  Europe is no stranger to these kinds of arrangements. In 1991, the European Community and Japan reached the so-called “Elements of Consensus” agreement, which called for a 9.4 per cent reduction in Japanese car exports to Europe. The current EU-China deal is thus a return to a familiar trade instrument. Because VERs are protectionism by another name, the World Trade Organization banned them under the 1995 Safeguards Agreement and required existing restraints to be phased out. But the WTO’s rules have since been weakened, not least by American officials’ blatant disregard for them. For Europe, the pressing question now is whether the quota makes economic sense, not whether it complies with WTO rules. With Chinese carmakers rapidly gaining market share, EU policymakers are under pressure to protect one of Europe’s biggest manufacturing industries and employers. The EU’s 2024 duties applied only to battery electric vehicles. Because its investigation did not cover hybrids, those remained subject to the standard 10 per cent tariff, and Chinese hybrid exports have since surged. A quota would enable the EU to show it is protecting domestic automakers without launching a new investigation.

For China, a quota has a distinct advantage over tariffs. While tariff revenue goes to European treasuries, a quota on Chinese exports allows Chinese producers to capture the increase in export prices. Both tariffs and quotas, however, reduce the volume of Chinese exports. Whether a quota is a good idea is contingent on what would happen without it. If the alternative is a US-style 100 per cent tariff on Chinese cars, then a quota is clearly preferable for both sides. European consumers would still have access to some Chinese cars, and Chinese firms could continue exporting to Europe rather than lose the market entirely. There is, however, a better alternative for the EU: A moderate tariff on Chinese hybrids and battery EVs, with the revenue used to subsidise car production in Europe. This would allow European consumers to continue buying low-cost, high-quality Chinese cars while helping domestic automakers make the transition to EVs, without adding to the EU’s fiscal burden. How China allocates export licences will determine the size of its net loss from the deal. One option is to award licences based on political or business connections. In a 2013 paper, Amit Khandelwal, Peter Schott, and I examined the quotas imposed on Chinese textile and clothing exports by the US, the EU, and other importing economies until 2005. We found that licences did not go to the most productive exporters. When the quotas were abolished, exports surged and prices fell as new firms entered the market. We also found that the way export quotas were administered essentially doubled the welfare loss to China. Another option is to issue export licences based on firms’ historical market shares, as Japan did in the 1980s and 1990s. This may create fewer opportunities for rent-seeking, but it still favours incumbents over potentially more efficient entrants. The third and most effective approach is to auction the licences. China’s auto industry is caught in a fierce price war, with more than 100 brands and widespread overcapacity. An auction system would encourage industry consolidation by squeezing out less efficient manufacturers while quota rents would boost government revenue. The car-export deal may well reduce China’s bilateral surplus with the EU, but it will do little to shrink its overall surplus, which exceeded $1 trillion in 2025 and reflects weak domestic consumption and high savings. Cars that Europe doesn’t want will simply go to Southeast Asia, Latin America, West Asia, or Africa. Brazil, Mexico, Turkey, and Thailand have already experienced a significant increase in Chinese imports, prompting some of them to raise tariffs. VERs are worse than tariffs for importers but better for exporters. Unlike tariffs, which generate revenue for importing countries, quotas let exporters pocket the resulting rents. The danger is that VERs tend to last long after they have served their purpose. The VERs imposed on Japan, for example, lasted more than a decade. Still, a VER is preferable to a prohibitive tariff—and even better if time-limited and allocated by auction. But that is an argument for carefully designed VERs in certain sectors, not a blank check for restricting trade.
